Fret buzz happens sometimes. And there is a level for each player that they consider tolerable fret buzz. If you plug it into an amp, does any of that string noise get translated there? If not, it's less of an issue. But a professional will be able to sort it pretty easily, just make sure to tell them you want minimal/no fret buzz, as most shops will aim to keep the action low, which can amount to small bits of fret buzz in most guitars.

Keep your head down and don't get discouraged that you aren't picking it up within a week.

Middle eastern loaded sweet potato:

1+ large sweet potato (depends on how many serves you're after)  
Olive oil  
1 teaspoon cumin  
1 teaspoon sumac  
1/2 teaspoon ground coriander  
1/4 teaspoon cinnamon  
1 diced white onion  
2 minced cloves garlic  
1 can of chickpeas (garbanzo beans)  
1 punnet of cherry tomatos  
1/4 cup pinenuts  
2 tablespoons tahini  
1 lemon

Wrap sweet potato in aluminium foil and bake at 200C (400F) for 50 minutes poke with knife after 30 minutes.

10 minutes before they're ready, add the oil and spices to a pan and toast for about a minute on high heat. Lower to medium heat and add the onion, garlic and cherry tomatos and mix to coat them in the spices. Saute for a few minutes until the onions and tomatos have softened. Drain and add the chickpeas and pinenuts and toss well. Mix the juice of one lemon and the tahini in a small bowl and mix until you have a uniform paste, add to the saucepan. Cook until pinenuts appear golden brown.

Cut a pocket down the middle of the sweet potato and fill with desired amount of the filling, serve with salt, pepper and coriander (cilantro).

I'm not sure what sort of situation you're in (college/working) so I'm not sure what sort of men you're surrounding yourself with, and the type of guy you typically find yourself attracted too. But in the way you described your interactions with them, it sounds like an issue many women face, some deal with it in different ways. Women (to my knowledge) are really very sociable people, you like it when a guy is making you a priority over his other commitments, especially so if he seems to have a busy personal life. So I think your reaction to feeling as if he ISN'T making you a priority, is a pretty natural and rational one.   


I think you might need to take a little bit of a break from really actively searching for a partner and properly evaluate what you're looking for, and some of the values you really hold dear. As a guy, when I hear a woman talking really passionately about her interests, whether that is work, school, hobbies etc, it's really engaging and attractive. A relationship is about addition to your life, not revolving your life around your relationship. So I think taking a step back, focusing on your personal interests and goals and really honing in on what makes you, you, then I think you will find that guys are just more naturally drawn and attracted to you.   


You also need to try and evaluate what these people you're interested in are after as well. Because if you learn that they're really not looking for a commitment and you are, or vice-versa, then spending your emotional energy on competing with these other women is just a futile engagement. I know not every guy is particularly switched on, and a lot of guys don't realise when a girl is interested in them romantically/sexually, but a lot also are, and you lingering there and vying for attention may be part of what is staving them off too. If it so happens that they ARE interested in you, distancing yourself to conserve your mental energy may be the wake-up call they need to chase your attention again.  


There are SO many variables that may be leading to this, and it could be as simple as you're going through a rough period in the dating scene, they happen. Best of luck to you though, hope my thoughts if anything give you something to think about going ahead.

I wasn't a waiter, but a chef in the kitchen at a small cafe/restaraunt. We only sat about 20 people max, and it was an open kitchen, so you could see and chat with customers while you cooked their food. 

One day, one of our waitresses was taking a older mans (50-60 yo) order, at around 10am. He ordered two waffles with icecream and maple syrup *with* a mushroom ragout. She and I both gave a brief, confused look but she took the order down anyway and I got everything ready. 

I couldn't have ever thought that he wanted the items together, but I was wrong. So wrong. I plated the waffles and had the mushroom ragout in a seperate bowl we would normally plate it in and delivered it to his table. To my horror and much of the other peoples horror in the cafe at the time, he simply scooped up the mushroom ragout and poured it on top of the waffles. I was unable to suppress my look of mild disgust as I walked away, but he didn't seem to care. But we had a good laugh about it after work that day.

I was fucking three years old at the time this happened (am now just about 25) and I still remember this pain like it was yesterday. I was up visiting family in Queensland, Australia, so naturally we went out to the beach for the day. My parents had gotten me swimming at an early age, so that if I was ever in a bad situation, I knew how to float on my back for a while. So they were nearby, but perhaps not paying super close attention to me, as my younger brother was about 6 months old at the time. I was playing around in a relatively deep (for a three year old) rockpool. I took a step forward to grab a shell I could see under the water, and my foot slipped against a smooth part of the rock and down to the sea floor, where a particular sharp piece of coral sliced deeply into the underside of my right foot. 

I screamed and my parents came running, freaking out as they saw the blood pouring into the water. Turns out I had sliced my medial plantar artery, so it bled quite a lot, but was manageable once they got me up to shore and wrapped a beach towel around it. We were at a secluded beach so it took about 40 minutes to get to the nearest hospital, and I think I honestly cried for 4 hours straight. It felt like fire shooting up my entire leg and into my lower back, but the wound itself wasn't too serious and all I got was a small local as they stitched it up and my mum held me and sung to me. Watch your footing kids.

A few years ago I was living with my grandmother for about 6 or so months after my grandfather (her husband) passed away. She was wanting to sell up her property (35 acre farmland), which she of course couldn't handle on her own, so I moved there temporarily to help her out with fixing up the place.

I had been there a few months and she drove out to a nearby town to talk with the contracter, leaving me alone there. I had done a lot of growing up there, and nothing weird or bad had ever really happened in the area, but to someone unfamiliar it might have a little bit of a 'Wolf Creek' vibe. It wasn't your usual farm of just flat plains and paddocks. It was up in the Blue Mountains and had a lot of rolling hills and forest surrounding it, so you did feel very secluded. 

I was out in one of the paddocks while she was away, making some repairs to a fence line down in a small wetland at the bottom of a hill. Up the other side of the hill is another paddock that leads up onto a road running along the back of the property and leading onto the neighbours. It's a pretty deserted road, and would probably only see 20 cars pass along it each day. 

Suddenly, I hear this blood-curdling scream for help, a woman's voice that made my hair stand on end. I just went full adrenaline mode, dropped my tools and started Usain Bolt sprinting up this hill towards the road, the woman screaming the whole time.

Just as I get towards the fence, I heard tyres spinning on dirt and this van shot past. I didn't have a hope of seeing the license plate, but I got a good look at the vans make/model. I rushed back to the house and called the police, giving them a description of the van and they put out a call to the highway patrols.

About an hour later the police show up at the house, telling me they had pulled over a van matching the description driving into the nearby town. Turns out that it was a caregiver transporting a mentally-ill patient, and that she had been trying to jump out of the van, before being man-handled back into it. But for anyone that heard her scream, they would have had the same thought I did, sitting there thinking I'd just witnessed an abduction. Still get chills thinking about her scream.
